newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-S&P's focus for NZ rating more on policy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-S&P's focus for NZ rating more on policy.

text.p: Ratings agency Standard & Poor's is watching the gradual evolution of the fiscal policy debate in New Zealand, and issues of debt repayment, but has little concern with short-term twists and turns in the economy as it assesses the ratings outlook, a top official said.

David Beers, managing director of S&P's soverign rating divison, was speaking on Friday as New Zealand money markets reacted sharply to current account data showing a record deficit of NZ$4.47 billion in the year to March.

He told Reuters that marketplace perceptions had brought short-term issues, such as how quickly the economy is slowing down, to the fore but such uncertainties had little relevance to ratings, especially as New Zealand has a relatively high long-term sovereign foreign currency rating of AA+, and the highest possible AAA rating for its local currency debt.

"From where I sit there is always a lot of uncertainty (about trends in the economy), all of this happens all of the time, everywhere. But does this have from our standpoint profound credit implications? No," he said.
He added the issue of a sustained fiscal policy course had improved New Zealand's rating up to now and would continue to.

"The government's persisting with something like the present course of policy that has sustained and improved the (sovereign) credit standing up to now -- that's what we've been saying for a long time is what's going to continue to sustain (the rating) going forward.
"Not whether the last quarter's GDP number grew or was flat, or is revised downwards next year," Beers said.

While S&P rises above the current market debates on the way monetary policy interacts with growth projections, and the possible impact on the level of future surpluses, Beers said S&P still believes robust fiscal supluses will continue.

In late June the six-month-old coalition government produced a budget which contained forecasts of budget surpluses going forward and re-stated an existing commitment to seek to reduce government debt.

While there had been some slippage in the level of surpluses forecast from those projected before the budget, as 1997 has proved to be a year of relatively sluggish growth, Beers said the shift had not changed S&P's stable outlook for the country. "We never expected ever-mounting surpluses...far ahead. I don't know anybody in this country who did -- even in the Treasury -- and neither did we."
S&P had upgraded New Zealand to AA-plus in early 1996, partly based on an expectation of what would happen over the next two or three years, he explained.

"And lo and behold what's been happening, in our view, is consistent with what we thought at the time. Our base case was that the surpluses would remain reasonably robust, even in a situation in which a coalition government was formed. So from our perspective that scenario has been fulfilled," Beers added.
Among the current issues that would influence the way S&P's outlook may change are the way the fiscal policy debate over the trade off between tax cuts and debt reduction pans out, he said.
"Part of the answer in our own minds, in terms of the rating outlook, is how that debate goes."

He said a clear policy decision to seek a further rate of decline in the ratio of net public external debt to exports "would certainly have an important impact it terms of our view on the possibility of an upgrade".

"That would imply that policy makers and the electorate are comfortable with surpluses persisting for a while yet and, therefore, the government's debt burden continuing to decline rapidly," he added.
